spans.s:
Vahatu is the regular name in the Rigveda and later for the ceremonial conducting of the bride from the house of her parents to that of her husband.
Foot notes i. 184, 3; iv. 58, 9; x. 17, 1 (= Av. iii. 31, 5); 32, 3; 85, 13 et seq.
Av. x. 1, 1; xiv. 2, 9, 12, 66, 73; aitareya brāhmaṇa, iv. 7, 1; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, i. 5, 1, 2.

Vahni, ‘carrier,’ denotes any draught animal--e.g., a ‘horse,’ a ‘goat,’ or an ‘ox.’
Foot notes Rv. ii. 24, 13; 37, 3; iii. 6, 2, etc.
Rv. vi. 57, 3.
taittirīya brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 2, 5, etc.

Vahya denotes in the Rigveda and the Atharvaveda a ‘couch’ or ‘bed’ of a comfortable kind used by women.
Foot notes vii. 55, 8.
iv. 5, 3; 20, 3; xiv. 2, 30.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 154.
Vāha is found in the Rigveda (iv. 57, 4. 8) and the Atharvaveda (vi. 102, 1) apparently denoting an ox for ‘drawing’ the plough. See also rathavāhana.

Vāhana (neut.) in the Brāhmaṇas denotes a ‘beast of burden,’ or occasionally a ‘cart.’ Cf. rathavāhana.
Foot notes aitareya brāhmaṇa, iv. 9, 4; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, i. 8, 2, 9; ii. 1, 4, 4; iv. 4, 4, 10.
Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, ix. 4, 2, 11.

Vāhasa, ‘boa constrictor,’ is included in the list of victims at the aśvamedha (‘horse sacrifice’) in the yajurveda Saṃhitās.
Foot notes taittirīya Saṃhitā, v. 5, 13, 1; 14, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 15; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 34. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 94.
